findings: The frozen Canonical contains three equivalent source variants asking for the difference between Spring Framework and Spring Boot. The candidate answers that relationship directly and covers all three variants without drifting into a separate auto-configuration-only question.

The central relationship is source-aligned: Spring Framework supplies the IoC/DI container and foundational application programming model, while Spring Boot builds Spring-based applications and reduces recurring application assembly and runtime setup through opinionated defaults and related conveniences. The answer does not incorrectly present Boot as a replacement for Spring Framework.

The candidate correctly separates starter dependencies from auto-configuration. Starters are described as convenient managed dependency descriptors, while auto-configuration is described as conditional default Spring configuration rather than as the same mechanism.

The auto-configuration boundary is accurate and important: defaults are conditional and non-invasive, user-defined configuration can cause defaults to back off, and specific auto-configurations can be excluded. The answer avoids describing auto-configuration as opaque or unconditional magic.

The runtime and production-ready section stays within the frozen official-source packet: stand-alone application patterns, common embedded-server combinations, externalized configuration, and Actuator health/metrics/auditing are presented as conveniences rather than as a guarantee of complete production governance.

The candidate includes the required concept comparison dimensions and confusion boundaries: it rejects XML-versus-annotation as the essential distinction, separates developer/setup efficiency from runtime performance, and explains that using Spring Boot does not itself constitute a complete microservice architecture.

No project migration, production incident, latency/QPS gain, or other personal experience is fabricated. The project section is explicitly framed as an application/verification mapping because the frozen source contains no user-specific project facts.

The one-minute section contains five main points and is suitable for oral recall. The three-minute section is intentionally thorough and may exceed a literal three-minute delivery, so oral quality is scored 4/5 rather than 5/5; this is not a semantic or promotion-blocking defect.
